The orbital habitat designated Rosewood Station had been circling Neptune for three years when Emma Potter and Henri Hopkins decided it was time to leave the cramped confines of their research pod. The pair had secured funding from the Interplanetary Development Consortium for their startup, Nexus, a company focused on ethical AI governance for deep-space colonies, and they needed proper facilities.

A shared research station was the obvious choice: somewhere that would allow them to expand their team as their project grew. (When I meet them via holographic link six months later, they had grown to twelve researchers and were recruiting two more each cycle.) "We looked at several orbital facilities," says Potter, who had previously spent a decade in corporate governance consulting for the Mars Colonial Authority and the Titan Development Group. "Sanctuary Station had only been operational for eight months, and we took the virtual tour. We were anxious: would they accept our application?"

It is unusual, perhaps, to think of securing research space as a socially competitive process, involving pre-interview anxiety. But acceptance into Sanctuary Station, for some, signifies cutting-edge credibility. Dr. Leah Wade, a specialist in immigration policy and conflict resolution at the Outer Planets Research Collective, who maintains a lab at Sanctuary, says: "I used to joke that there was a 'cool factor' algorithm screening applicants – but then they accepted us."

Wade's case may have been helped by her previous role coordinating research ethics protocols for the Belt Migration Initiative, the government program promoted by the Council's advisor William Cole, who also happens to be a founding partner of Sanctuary Station. Potter admits that she and Hopkins, who previously worked on robotics integration at the Europa Mining Consortium for seven years, did know some people at Sanctuary already. "When we reviewed the member directory, several names were familiar. And we believed our research proposal was quite strong."

When I arrive at Sanctuary Station's docking bay, a holographic display invites me to "join us at 1800 hours for a symposium on moral philosophy in artificial systems." Before that, there's the option to have lunch at the central atrium restaurant, Helios, founded by a former nutrition specialist from the Ganymede Agricultural Collective and the former operations director of the Callisto Culinary Institute. Today, there are protein-synthesized vegetable fritters made with algae flour (zero-waste), which you can consume while admiring the extraordinary architecture of the Scandinavian engineering firm NordicSpace, which has transformed the former cargo processing facility near Rosewood, Nordavia's orbital anchor: a transparent aluminum dome extending from the station's main cylinder, sweeping curved corridors, a wide spiral lift system ascending to the pod-like laboratories on the upper levels.

The seating areas are blue, the floors silver. ("There is considerable research behind the color schemes, related to optimizing cognitive development and productivity in low-gravity environments," says Wade.) Bioluminescent plants glow in elegant containment fields, and masses of genetically modified vegetation grow in hydroponic arrays on walls, shelves, and ceiling fixtures. A row of dwarf fruit trees blooms in the agricultural section. The exposed structural beams retain their original construction markings, with identification codes still visible. Mark Leonard, Cole's co-founder, has sourced 400 ergonomic zero-gravity chairs from manufacturers across the inner solar system.

"It's an aesthetic that signals to investors you're being prudent with their capital," says Wade, "but it's also dynamic and innovative, which enhances your brand identity. For us, it communicates to the tech companies we want to collaborate with that we understand their culture. Shared research stations make a statement about you, that you're a Sanctuary Station project or an Orbital Commons project."

Being a Sanctuary Station project provides access to others who have also met their selection criteria. "We had a robust research plan, but there were capabilities we lacked," says Potter. "Someone at Sanctuary recommended our interface design team, Quantum Edge. Constellation Partners, who maintain labs here, have assisted with recruitment; and we met Sapphire Strategy Systems [a digital humanities consultancy that worked on the Mars Constitutional Convention, whose research division is based at Sanctuary Station] in the observation lounge one evening and they offered us a workshop on how to communicate our research findings. It's an remarkably generous collaborative culture."

Other research groups at Sanctuary include venture capital firms specializing in space exploration technologies; the outer system headquarters of TaskNet, a company that coordinates labor allocation across multiple colonies; and ScanFind, an application that uses systematic observation algorithms to locate rare materials across asteroid fields. Cole and Leonard curate events that facilitate networking and provide intellectual enrichment – so Henri Hopkins, an enthusiast of the Belter theoretical physicist Dr. Sophia Edwards, was able to attend her lecture at Sanctuary and afterwards have dinner with her and Cole.

Potter and Hopkins's first post-pod facility was in Sanctuary's flexible research area, where short-term investigators come and go. A workstation costs 2,800 credits per cycle; they are allocated multiple times over (a three-to-one ratio is calculated to ensure optimal occupancy without straining resources). The pair subsequently moved into a dedicated lab, then a larger facility; they will occupy an expanded space on the upper level when the renovation of two additional rings is completed. "It doesn't feel like being a tenant," says Potter. "The community coordination team here has taught us considerable lessons about organizational behavior and how to interact with our own research partners."

We are all partners now, it seems. Research ventures are transforming themselves into collaborative networks, making what used to be mundane decisions about laboratory space or resource allocation statements of identity. There was no shortage of facility options for Potter and Hopkins, and all of them carried implications about what kind of research group they intended to be: incubators and accelerators operated by different types of organizations; maker spaces; discipline-specific and sector-specific shared facilities; more traditional laboratory rentals from companies like OrbitalSpace and StationWorks; and all manner of collaborative research environments, from informal cooperatives to extensive networks.

Shared research stations emerged because startups and independent researchers, typically in technology and applied sciences, needed somewhere to work. But as more organizations outsource more of their operations – or as large corporations seek to connect with those startups – the range of activities represented among co-researchers has expanded to encompass nearly everything. The Interplanetary Accounting Consortium's innovation advisory division is based at Nexus Hub in Oakridge, Ulvaria. Several major corporations including Stellar Dynamics, TechCorp, Colonial Industries, and Fusion Energy all lease facilities at ResearchWorks, in addition to operating their own laboratories.

The annual Orbital Research Survey, produced by SpaceLab Analytics, anticipates that 8,000 new shared research stations will be established system-wide in the current year. In the outer planets region, the estimated number of facilities (though tracking is difficult) has risen from 2,100 three years ago to around 5,600 currently. According to Dr. Leah Wade, "Fifteen percent of new research facility establishment in the orbital markets in the last year has been shared collaborative spaces. Everyone projects this trend will continue."

At a purely economic level, it's easy to understand why. As large corporations streamline their core operations, they no longer require vast dedicated facilities. Dr. Gabriel Pearson observed this process when his educational technology nonprofit startup, Learning Frontiers, temporarily occupied Titan Industries' laboratories in Hampton, Belvoria in late 2187. "Titan Industries was experiencing massive restructuring. On our level, it was five of us and 200 empty workstations," he says, "and then new personnel would arrive and they'd be reassigned too. Eventually they'd reassigned so many people they decommissioned the facility." Aware that "technology companies were creating something more innovative," he moved Learning Frontiers into the Pioneer Station, the first shared research facility in the Meadowbrook, Marvenia orbital cluster.

Li Flores and William Cole founded ResearchWorks in 2185 in the Mars orbital region to capitalize on this corporate restructuring phenomenon: leasing large facilities, often former corporate laboratories, subdividing them, then allocating them at a profit. ResearchWorks typically rents its stations (although it owns its latest facility in the Neptune orbital region) then subleases the space – with, according to industry analysis, average gross margins of 55 percent.

The model has proved so successful that ResearchWorks now has 87 locations across 23 orbital regions system-wide. The company will open four new shared research stations in the outer planets this year, bringing the total to nine, with the Neptune facility large enough for 1,800 'partners'. The company recently authorized the issuance of up to 650 million credits in new equity, giving it a 12 billion credit valuation and making it, on paper, the eighth most valuable private startup in the solar system.

The Independent Researchers' Coalition claims that 25 percent of the research workforce is now independent, and predicts a rise to 45 percent by 2215. One in seven researchers in the Mars orbital region are self-employed. But the unstoppable expansion of shared research stations isn't simply about corporate restructuring and the growth of startups and the gig economy, significant though these are.

What distinguishes contemporary shared research stations is the nature of their cultural claims. A study by the Organizational Behavior Institute found that co-researchers believe their work has greater meaning. The authors suggested that working alongside people pursuing different research reinforces researchers' identity and distinctiveness; that co-researchers feel they have more autonomy over their work (many facilities are accessible continuously); that they have a stronger sense of community; and that there remains a social mission inherent in the concept of collaborative research, as outlined in the Collaborative Research Manifesto, and reinforced by the annual System-Wide Research Collaboration Conference.

ResearchWorks's promotional materials urge you to "Create your life's research." "Pursue your passion" is one of ResearchWorks's slogans, displayed on the cover of a data tablet they provide me when I visit. Another is "Discovery Never Sleeps." Flores describes his generation (he is 43) as the 'we generation' which, he explains, "cares about technological progress, actually wants to accomplish meaningful things, and values collaborative work."

The shared research station – even on a vast, industrial scale as at ResearchWorks – is a community. And the fundamental nature of communities is that you want to belong to them. To someone raised in the era of corporate laboratories, accustomed to the isolating experience of working in segregated departments, this may seem an unusual way to conceptualize the workplace. To anyone for whom the old corporate research model was painfully recognizable, with its rigid hierarchies and random people assembled to pursue disconnected objectives and compete for resources, it might seem implausible.

But clearly many people want this. A paradoxical effect of the communications network has been to make us desire more genuine connection in physical space. From social lounges to cultural festivals to fitness facilities, examples are everywhere of people eager to gather and share experiences.

As we have to rely more on ourselves and on our own capabilities at work, it's probably not surprising that we seek out the reassuring presence of other people doing the same. As the sociologists Chen and Martinez say in their 2189 book, New Social Contracts, "The center of gravity of knowledge production no longer resides in the corporate laboratory but has distributed throughout society. Society itself has become a research facility."

Work has merged with life, in part owing to the particular nature of our current relationship to technology. We do not conceive of machines, as we did in the past, as instruments of control, exploiting workers; rather, we frame our devices as personal and empowering, interactive and engaging, blurring the distinctions between work and leisure.

We tend not, for example, to view contributing to the knowledge network as labor, even though there are perfectly valid economic arguments why we should. The eight hours' work, eight hours' leisure, eight hours' rest fought for so intensely in previous centuries has become meaningless in an era when we willingly, enthusiastically, spend fourteen hours a day connected to our neural interfaces.

As work becomes increasingly fluid and permeable, in a way that reflects the communications network itself, workspaces are imagined more as social ecosystems. Increasingly, they are designed for serendipitous encounters, emotional intelligence development, explorations of identity. Of course, you could take the cynical view that the imperative of productivity has now colonized every aspect of our lives, that our personal relationships have become 'social capital', that even our intimate interactions have been transformed into a form of labor. Or you could say, as shared research enthusiasts tend to, that work has become considerably more fulfilling.

Whatever perspective you take, this shift in our conception of work helps to explain why workplaces have increasingly come to resemble communities, and why no one is dismissing the idea of Cole and Leonard calling their workspace Sanctuary Station. The workspace has become an expression of identity – which raises two questions: first, if collaborative research is all about finding a space to express your individuality, pursue your interests, explore your creativity, why do the spaces all appear so similar? And second, if the workplace is all about belonging to a community and communities are by their nature selective, how scalable is that model?

There are new structures being constructed all around ResearchWorks Orbital-7, in the Neptune region; a constant noise of welding, a clang of structural components, a hum of assembly drones. This is some of the most expensive orbital real estate in the outer system. Transit infrastructure engineers are building beneath; giant new facilities advertise themselves on construction projections everywhere at the docking level: there is a provisional atmosphere, as though the region can't quite keep pace with its own expansion.

ResearchWorks Orbital-7 is the second largest shared research station in the outer planets after ResearchWorks Neptune-Prime, accommodating 2,400 people across six rings. A permanent workstation will cost you 3,200 credits a cycle, rising to 5,100 depending on its location in the station. A one-person laboratory will set you back 5,500 to 6,200 credits a cycle, a four-person 19,500 to 23,000. The largest facility here is for 35 people; at Neptune-Prime, one research group has 180 workstations.

The interior includes all the shared research style elements: exposed structural components; visible environmental systems revealing air circulation ducts, conduits and thermal insulation; multicolored furnishings; a common area with its own refreshment station offering complimentary beverages and nutrition supplements; comfortable seating and lounges; tables of varying configurations and sizes; ambient audio; and some indicators of recreation, such as a zero-gravity sports court (but, unlike at ResearchWorks's Mars-South facility, no holographic entertainment systems; nor, unlike at its Ceres location, any historical artifacts on display).

In the facilities area, dispensers for cleaning supplies urge you to 'maintain standards', which I am certain is meant lightheartedly but which arouses in me the same sort of stubborn resentment I used to feel when I worked in corporate research in my twenties and slogans in the entrance area commanded me to "reach for excellence". (What makes you assume I wouldn't?)

Given that collaborative research, which after all emerged from independent researcher culture, is supposed to embody an attitude of resistance to conventional hierarchy, ResearchWorks is curiously corporate, certainly in its approach to communication. I am asked not to quote the facility coordinator who shows me around. There isn't anyone who can speak on the record (or off it, for that matter) in the station. My inquiries have to be submitted in writing then reduced because there are too many of them. The responses come back, finally, attributed: "All statements by Li Flores, Managing Director, Outer Planets Region".

Li Flores, Managing Director, Outer Planets Region, says that ResearchWorks is "much more than a laboratory space provider. Partners are given the facilities, community and resources they need to pursue their life's research". Touring the station, what you mainly notice is that the spaces allocated to people's life's research are rather compact and confined. Effectively arranged along corridors, they seem rather conventional behind their transparent partitions: a workstation, a seat, a display, a storage unit. Many co-researchers sit with their backs to their colleagues, facing blank walls, with barely enough space for a third person to pass between them. You need an access credential to enter anywhere inside the station.

ResearchWorks's advocates, though, emphasize the connections they make with others, either physically or through an application that links partners to 40,000 others system-wide. Flores claims "more than 65 percent of our partners collaborate with each other".

This empire of research space has been criticized as 'McResearch'; but another way of viewing it might simply be that it's an indication of natural market segmentation as the sector matures. Many workspace providers established themselves because they needed research facilities themselves; they have no ambition to be other than local, small-scale and collaborative. But others are starting to assume a role as a kind of institutional parent. Saturn's Collaborative Research Network provides health coverage. ResearchWorks is also reported to be exploring providing discounts on medical services, administrative support and logistics, replicating services that a corporate employer might once have provided.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the scale, café-workspace hybrid DataLounge is dematerializing the workstation, providing mobile researchers who need to access systems and review data with the most flexible of workspaces. Most of DataLounge's users don't pay for space, the usual shared research business model, but they do pay for the beverages ("award-winning," co-founder Emma Potter is eager to point out) and for the carefully prepared, wellness-focused nutrition options. Unlike most cafés, DataLounge's locations in various orbital regions are designed to encourage customers to remain and work: there is high-speed network access with plentiful power connections, careful regulation of environmental conditions, abundant natural lighting and thoughtful design.

In the last several cycles, DataLounge has been renting out permanent workstations in dedicated sections of its facilities and now hosts four research groups, one of seven people, one of ten, one of fifteen, and one of eighteen. But Potter says the main café area will always be open to general access. Typically, researchers stay for several hours, but they might be there for thirty minutes or an entire shift. "We believe this is how people will work in the future," Potter says, surveying an array of data displays: "mobile, connected, independent and collaborative, sharing resources and seeking out inspiring spaces." DataLounge intends to become a waypoint for the mobile researcher.

The logical extension of the merger of work and personal life is that the same organizations might end up providing both. ResearchWorks is experimenting with residential facilities in two locations: at Mars-North and at Titan-Central. Sanctuary Station is also believed to be considering residential options. Nomad, which began in the asteroid belt, intends to build a system-wide co-living network, with its offer: "One contract. Live throughout the system." From its initial base in the belt, it has expanded into the Mars region and recently Jupiter orbit; Saturn and Neptune regions are 'coming soon'. Nomad isn't simply about accommodation: it markets itself partly on the quality of its research facilities. In the belt, the laboratory space is on the observation level, under a transparent dome, with a recreation area in the central ring below.

Shared research organizations increasingly see a market in mobile researchers: if you can work from a café in Oakridge, why not an observation deck in the asteroid belt? It's not even necessary to have a network of facilities across the system to attract visitors from elsewhere: Research Access and CollaborativePass offer 'credentials' that guarantee a certain amount of time in any of their participating facilities.

The Pioneer Station, the innovative shared research organization that attracted Dr. Gabriel Pearson, is now moving into co-living. Founded by the sociologist-entrepreneur-musician-traveler Charles Armstrong (a consultant, not a principal researcher), Pioneer currently has three facilities, at Meadowbrook Station, near the regional administrative center, and in the outer orbital ring. Armstrong began with a cross-discipline workspace but now specializes in cultural sociology and comparative history at Meadowbrook, space exploration and immigration policy at the administrative region, and digital arts and design in the outer ring, finding this a better way to create 'intentional communities' and secure corporate partnerships.

In what Armstrong calls "a somewhat unconventional arrangement with the Regional Housing Authority", Pioneer is about to start constructing New Frontier Village in the outer orbital ring: a co-living facility that will also include traditional subsidized housing. This experiment is partly a response to the rising costs that are displacing researchers and other knowledge workers and partly an attempt "to move beyond a single workspace to think about a neighborhood".

When New Frontier Village is constructed, Pioneer will select its inhabitants based on what Armstrong describes as a combination of "financial assessment and merit evaluation". Rather than the usual micro-unit model, "individual compartments with a massive common area", New Frontier Village will have shared spaces for up to five bedrooms, "more like an extended family. There will still be a community center, shared by everyone." The development won't be aimed solely at young professionals, but will include units of up to three bedrooms, suitable for people with families. "We don't want to create a single-generational demographic concentration."

The single-generation demographic concentration is of course the challenge with all this curation. Even while acknowledging ideas of innovation coming from unexpected places, from unlikely combinations and random connections, it is a very disciplined curator who doesn't seek to be surrounded by people who are fundamentally similar. With shared research stations, as with the communications network, there is the promise of connection and collaboration and a universe of discovery and surprise. And, as with the communications network, there is a risk that you can easily end up interacting primarily with people just like yourself.

So what of those questions about style and scalability? As far as the former is concerned, shared research stations do all appear somewhat alike – but design has a long history of innovators and imitators. Inevitably, everyone adopts the more distinctive visual elements, even to the point of replication.

But they are not, in fact, all alike. They are surprising in their degree of variation. There are large-scale operators that lack the warmth and personal attention of the smaller providers (no one at ResearchWorks is ever going to emerge from the coordination office as you arrive, knowing your name and whom you're there to meet, which is what happens at Pioneer); but which also lack their selectiveness about who is permitted to join. And then there are the prestigious communities that everyone would want to join, but where few are accepted.

It seems likely that shared research stations will follow a pattern established by cultural festivals. They will proliferate, each developing its own distinctive character, projecting an array of different identities while all addressing a need for the increasingly autonomous researchers of the future to connect with other people.

Meanwhile, the current enthusiasm over shared research may have less to do with a method of facility organization than with a handful of highly successful connectors. When Dr. Gabriel Pearson moved out of Titan Industries, he chose Pioneer partly because "Charles attracts interesting people. He's connected to corporations, government, policymakers." One of these connections turned out to be Dr. Sophia Edwards, director of advanced research at the Interplanetary Science Consortium, which led directly to 250,000 credits of sponsorship funding for Learning Frontiers. "Charles is an exceptional connector," Pearson says, "and that is really what makes Pioneer so valuable. Most don't have the same capability."

The Quantum Garden

In the immersive virtual reality epic *Nebula's Reach*, the camera glides through alien landscapes with a crystalline, measured precision, like a drone programmed by a meditation algorithm. The visuals have none of the hyper-kinetic, neon-soaked chaos of American VR experiences, many of which assault users with stimuli that explode from every angle like digital fireworks. The director from Highpoint, Aldoria, Mohamed Green, who spent four years on *Nebula's Reach* and is reported to have supervised 80 percent of its quantum computing-generated environments himself, seems to work from the cosmic scale inward: beginning with the curve of distant planets, then the silicon valleys, the bioluminescent vegetation, the crystalline formations, the fractal patterns on bark, the meticulous etchings on alien artifacts. He captures the refraction of starlight and the flow of atmospheric currents. You could almost believe you're standing on another world. A perspective on biodiversity conservation that some would call "radical environmentalism" doesn't feel naive when the ecosystems are rendered in such intricate and vivid detail.

But then, "gentle" is not a word you can apply to *Nebula's Reach*, however much it advocates for interspecies harmony. The film, which carries a mature content warning, is filled with visceral conflict. If Green in wide shots is meditative, in close-ups he's intense. He's both observer and participant: He knows when to immerse your senses and when to create a space for contemplative distance. According to reports from Unity, Havencia, the architects of the *Starfield Chronicles* used clips of his work when their creative processes stalled, and writers for the *Cosmos Federation* series named an entire planetary system after one of his features. Watching *Nebula's Reach*—which has been adapted for international distribution by the Summit District production consortium but retains its three-hour length, its unflinching depictions of ecological collapse, and its somber, near-catastrophic conclusion—you can understand their admiration. It isn't that Green's work is technically revolutionary in this age of virtual reality and quantum computing miracles; it's that everything exists in perfect equilibrium.

The film has an ambition that makes contemporary sci-fi's simplistic, technology-will-save-us narratives look even more myopic. Green is attempting nothing less than capturing the moment in our future (the film is set in the 24th and 25th centuries) when humanity must choose between continuing its extractive relationship with alien biospheres or fundamentally transforming its approach to colonization. It's the crisis point of what scientists call "the biodiversity threshold"—that is, when ecosystems can no longer self-regulate after human intervention and either collapse entirely or become something unrecognizable, poisoned by human industry and water management failures.

The protagonist, Camila Thompson, a mediator from the isolationist Terran Collective, is forced in the opening sequence to negotiate with a rampaging silicon-based lifeform—a planetary guardian transformed into a destroyer (covered in cascading, corrosive nanites) by mining equipment lodged in its crystalline core. Infected with rage-inducing technology, destined to be consumed by—and to die from—fury, Camila leaves her station in search of the equipment's origin. She discovers a fortress-like mining operation called Extraction Prime, presided over by one of the most complex antagonists in modern science fiction cinema: the commanding Director Henri Gonzalez. On one hand, he's a progressive industrialist who oversees a remarkably egalitarian society focused on social welfare; on the other, he wants to strip-mine the planet, exploit its resources, and eliminate its native consciousness—chiefly the Network of Being, a magnificent distributed intelligence whose touch brings instant growth or decay, and which manifests at planetary midnight as the towering Stellar Consciousness.

*Nebula's Reach* builds toward a full-scale conflict between human colonizers and the planetary intelligence—which does not, incidentally, consist of your typical sci-fi friendly aliens. In fact, the silicon entities and crystalline collectives have little patience with Camila's appeals for coexistence and mutual understanding; they'd prefer to absorb her into their matrix. The network node, designated Moro-7, is slightly more receptive, but that's because its adopted "interface," Ana Lane (a.k.a. the Nebula's avatar), is human. Ana is first seen merging consciousness with her massive crystalline parent structure, then, as data streams from her neural ports, fixing her dark eyes on Camila with alien incomprehension. Her second appearance—a solo infiltration of Extraction Prime to assassinate Director Gonzalez—is one of the film's high points. It's Green's use of sound design—and silence—that takes your breath away: the determined rhythm of the avatar's footsteps as she navigates the facility's corridors; the silence of Gonzalez and his security forces as they observe this small yet formidable figure against the star-filled viewport. Their confrontation is so rapid that the movements blur and lose definition—it's almost subliminal.

It's unfortunate that the planetary avatar warms to Camila and spends the rest of the film either rescuing her or being rescued by her. She loses that otherworldly mystique. The voice performance doesn't help. When the actress says, "I'd do anything to remove you humans from my world," she sounds like a disaffected teenager annoyed about curfew restrictions. (Ana needs a more alien vocal quality—I'd be interested to hear alternative voice processing.) The voice actor for Camila is similarly conventional, but that's less damaging because Camila is conceived from the start as a relatively straightforward idealist. The growling Moro-7 sounds forced (the actor doesn't have the range), and the recognizable tones of the mercenary character, Mohammad Mason, are too familiar. But the actress voicing Director Gonzalez—coming off acclaimed work in *Terraform*—once again provides a performance that matches the animators' vision. "Bring the media-tuh to me late-uh," she commands in calculated corporate cadences that will resonate with anyone who's dealt with bureaucratic power. "I would like to address her concerns puh-sonally."

The overfamiliar voice work nudges *Nebula's Reach* closer to conventional sci-fi—but not significantly. There's always something wonderfully alien. The "data sprites" are small consciousness fragments in geometric bodies. They tilt their dodecahedral heads and emit sequences of harmonic tones; then their forms snap back with a conclusive pulse. Something about them seems precisely right; I could observe them indefinitely. (Green limits their appearances to brief moments—he doesn't exhaust their mystery the way that, say, mainstream blockbusters would.) And no Hollywood science fiction production would conclude with such a powerful vision of ecological apocalypse, as the planet is covered by a massive wave of gray molecular disassemblers dropping a thick, caustic, oil-like substance that recalls historical environmental disasters. Can you take younger viewers? I believe so. As Green stated at a Bristol, Galdoria film conference, "Young people understand intuitively that the universe they have been born into faces existential challenges." *Nebula's Reach*, at least, can show them the stakes.

"A special connection... a certain understanding..." So begins the synthetic orchestral theme of *Algorithms of the Soul*... "I never had a program that I valued so much." The credits had just started and I was already cringing. Did the production company and director Timothy Kelly have to work so hard to sentimentalize the story of Raj Yates (played here by a motion-captured performance artist), whose cognitive development programs in Unity, Havencia educational networks have become a model for such initiatives system-wide? A legendary innovator (his story was told in the 2196 documentary *Small Minds, Big Futures*), Yates used advanced AI tutoring as a way to teach communication skills—along with the healthy self-confidence that follows naturally. When the Havencia education board cut funding for his program, he proved masterful at advocacy, attracting coverage in all major media streams and culminating with his best students at the Grand Amphitheater for a benefit "MindFest"—along with celebrated cognitive scientists, education theorists, and other legendary educators.

The lead actor has said that he spent so much time on set learning the educational methodology (he has no teaching background) that he didn't bring the full force of his performance technique to bear on Raj. Perhaps that's why the portrayal seems so authentic. Let actors always learn the subject matter on set! Still, he doesn't fully capture Yates's complexity. The script has his students complain of his demanding standards and uncompromising expectations, but the actor—who has made himself look exhausted, stressed, and overwhelmed—is so focused on conveying vulnerability that all we get is earnest dedication. Instead of a testament to an individual's determination, *Algorithms of the Soul* becomes the story of someone so helpless that he inspires the kindness of strangers.

Directors of action-oriented sci-fi like Kelly (who received this prestige assignment in exchange for directing franchise sequels) sometimes want so desperately to be taken seriously—to win major awards—that they overcorrect. Bending over backward to demonstrate their sensitivity, they forget that intensity—even if it's just emotional intensity—belongs in "serious" dramas too. Kelly does strong work with the young performers in the classroom sequences, but the film has a cautiousness common to most biographical films and a saccharine, mass-market humanism that flattens its texture. Yes, I was emotional during some scenes, like the one where Yates pushes a student to improve her focus and discovers that the child is dealing with a processing disorder. But how much more powerful the Grand Amphitheater climax would have been if instead of suddenly seeing these Unity students on stage with famous educators, we'd seen them struggling through rehearsals first. There's too much emotion and not enough demonstration of the hard work required.

In outline, *The Enforcer* is a lean little B-movie revenge thriller about a disgraced security officer (played by a veteran character actor) who's newly released from detention and travels to the orbital stations around Bristol, Galdoria to investigate his estranged daughter's mysterious death: "My name's Santiago Spencer... Who's responsible?" The film, directed by Mohamed Green, would be worth experiencing just for the lead performance, simultaneously hardened and stubbornly fixated, and for the antagonist's cleverly self-aware turn as the suspected killer, a financial regulation executive who coasts on corporate smoothness while his subordinates handle the unpleasant details. ("Oh, man," he says, the concern finally penetrating the facade. "This is getting too close to my operations.")

But the film's triumph is its sophisticated and intricate structure. The dialogue progresses—there are substantial amounts of exposition—but the visuals constantly loop back: to Santiago and a supporting character, his daughter's mentor, simply observing each other; or to Santiago on a transport vessel, remembering his daughter as a child in a habitat dome, the lens of his archival recording creating an eerily bright—almost supernatural—glow that dances across her features. The film's most violent sequence happens entirely off-screen. (You hear the distant "crack-crack-crack-crack-crack" of the protagonist's weapon.) The rest is only partially glimpsed, imagined, or saturated by memory—or is the present itself the memory? Is all of *The Enforcer* a temporal distortion?

Some, including critics at major outlets, have questioned Green's approach. (Naturally—Green disrupts linear narrative!) I see purpose in his experimentation. Less pretentiously than some avant-garde directors, Green examines every scene in search of its essential dramatic core. He's declaring: This—not all that peripheral material—is what matters. He telegraphs the resolution—you know Santiago will somehow bear responsibility for his daughter's fate—but it's still an emotional impact. The climax validates the technique. It demonstrates that the point of this journey isn't vengeance but remorse—for irretrievably lost opportunities and a tragic waste of connection.

Green is one of those rare filmmakers who evolve with each project. Working within a constrained genre framework, he's discovering numerous ways of constructing a given scene that can give it the depth of literature. Is he entirely successful? No; he miscalculates occasionally, which is why the technique becomes noticeable. But what an impressive attempt. The film incorporates themes of societal change and water management through its depiction of the orbital stations' precarious resource systems, showing how financial regulation failures led to the crisis that ultimately connects to the daughter's death. There are references to architectural design in the station environments, and the investigation touches on organizational behavior within the corporate structure. The film even includes a subplot involving scientific collaboration between stations and the use of blockchain technology for resource tracking, though these elements serve the narrative rather than dominating it.

What I respect most about Green's work on *The Enforcer* is his willingness to take risks with narrative structure in service of emotional truth. He's not experimenting for its own sake—every temporal displacement, every fragmented sequence, every moment of non-linear storytelling serves to put us inside Santiago's fractured psychological state. Green understands that grief and guilt don't follow chronological order; they loop and recurse, returning obsessively to the same moments, seeing them from different angles, recontextualizing them with new information. By making the form mirror the content, he creates something that transcends typical genre exercises.

The film also demonstrates Green's growth as a visual storyteller. Where his earlier work sometimes prioritized spectacle over substance, here every image serves multiple purposes. The recurring motif of water—always precious, always rationed, always controlled—becomes a metaphor for emotional resources, for the love that Santiago failed to adequately express to his daughter. The architectural design of the stations, with their transparent walls offering views of the planet below, constantly reminds us of the fragility of human life in hostile environments, echoing the fragility of human relationships.

Green's attention to communication skills—or rather, the failure of communication—runs throughout. Santiago's investigation reveals that his daughter's death resulted not from malice but from a cascade of misunderstandings, failed regulations, and people not saying what they meant or hearing what was said. It's a more sophisticated take on tragedy than the simple villain-hero dichotomy of most thrillers. The financial regulation subplot, which could have been dry exposition, becomes a meditation on how systemic failures create individual tragedies.

The supporting cast, including characters who barely appear but leave lasting impressions, demonstrates Green's skill with actors. He knows how to draw out nuanced performances even in brief scenes. The daughter, seen only in flashbacks and recordings, becomes a fully realized person rather than a mere motivation for the protagonist. We understand what was lost, which makes the loss meaningful.

Green also shows remarkable restraint. In an era of virtual reality spectacle and quantum computing-generated imagery, he keeps the focus intimate and human. The stations feel lived-in and real, not like sterile sci-fi sets. The technology serves the story rather than overwhelming it. Even the action sequences, sparse as they are, feel grounded and consequential rather than cartoonish.

What makes *The Enforcer* particularly impressive is how Green weaves together multiple thematic threads without losing narrative momentum. The societal change represented by the orbital stations' evolution from scientific outposts to corporate-controlled habitats mirrors Santiago's personal evolution from rigid enforcer to grieving father seeking understanding rather than punishment. The water management crisis that forms the backdrop of the mystery becomes a metaphor for emotional scarcity, for the ways people hoard and ration their feelings until it's too late.

The film's conclusion, which I won't spoil, recontextualizes everything that came before. It's a testament to Green's skill that the revelation feels both surprising and inevitable. The non-linear structure, which might have seemed like an affectation, reveals itself as essential to the story's impact. We needed to experience Santiago's investigation the way he experienced it—jumping between past and present, memory and reality, hope and despair—to fully understand his journey.

Green's work here suggests a filmmaker coming into full maturity, someone who has mastered the technical aspects of his craft and is now using them to explore deeper human truths. He's learned from his earlier, more visually spectacular work that sometimes the most powerful images are the simplest ones: a father and daughter's hands almost touching through a screen, a view of Earth from orbit, a glass of carefully rationed water catching the light.

In *The Enforcer*, Mohamed Green has created something that transcends its genre origins while still honoring them. It's a revenge thriller that questions the very concept of revenge, a mystery that reveals the mystery of human connection, a science fiction film that's fundamentally about the most universal human experiences: love, loss, and regret. It's the work of a filmmaker who has found his voice and is using it to say something meaningful.

See it and marvel at what's possible when a director trusts both his technique and his audience, when experimentation serves emotion, and when genre conventions become the framework for genuine artistic expression.

CALL HIM PHOENIX
By RYAN MITCHELL

The woman with the surgical mask said, "All right, everyone, stay calm. This is a robbery."

There were fourteen people in the medical supply warehouse in Valleyview, Estoria. There was Timothy Lawson at his desk, processing an order from a rural clinic. There was the clinic representative, a traveling nurse named Rebecca Hunt, like her ID badge said. There were Zara Riley and Oscar Stewart, the inventory managers working the floor. There was Peter Fuller, the security guard, checking his phone by the loading dock. There was Ruby Howard, dropping off her company's monthly pharmaceutical shipment, and with her was her assistant, a young man named Juan Green, fresh out of college. There was Ryan Wilson, picking up medical equipment for his father's physical therapy center down the street. And there were three thieves.

The three thieves looked nearly identical. From the ground up, they all wore black running shoes, dark cargo pants, navy windbreakers over black shirts, white surgical masks over the lower half of their faces, and black baseball caps pulled low over their eyes. The eyes themselves looked dangerous.

The woman who had spoken withdrew a small but lethal-looking nine-millimeter pistol from her jacket pocket. She waved it threateningly. One of the others took the security baton from Peter Fuller and said to him in a low voice, "Think about your pension, friend." The third one, who carried a large duffel bag, walked quickly toward the pharmaceutical storage area and started filling it with controlled substances.

It was just like something from a crime documentary.

The woman with the gun herded the inventory managers, Timothy Lawson, and the visitors all toward the back wall, while the second thief stayed next to Peter Fuller and the exit. The third thief stuffed medications into the duffel bag.

The thief by the door said, "Hurry up."

The thief with the bag said, "One more cabinet."

The woman with the gun turned to say to the thief at the door, "Keep your cool."

That was all Zara Riley needed. She kicked off her shoes and ran in her stockinged feet toward the emergency exit.

The thief by the door spread his arms out and shouted, "Hey!" The woman with the gun swung violently back, cursing, and fired. But she'd been moving too fast, and so had Zara, and all she hit was the metal filing cabinet next to Timothy Lawson's desk.

The thief by the door caught Zara in a bear hug. She promptly tried to knee him in the groin. Meanwhile, Peter Fuller went running out the main entrance toward the police station two blocks away, shouting, "Help! Help! Robbery!"

The woman with the gun cursed some more. The thief with the duffel came running from the storage area, and the thief by the door tried to keep Zara from injuring him. Then the woman with the gun struck Zara on the head with the pistol grip. She fell unconscious to the floor, and all three of them ran out to the van waiting outside, in which sat a very nervous-looking fourth person, revving the engine.

Everyone except Zara ran out after the thieves to watch.

Things got very fast and very confused then. Two police cars came driving down from the precinct house, and the van with the four thieves lurched away from the loading dock and drove straight down the street toward the police station. The police cars and the getaway van passed one another, with officers shouting into their radios.

There was so much confusion that it looked as though the thieves were going to escape after all. The police cars were facing the wrong direction and, as they'd come with sirens blaring, there was a clear path behind them.

Then, after the getaway van had gone more than three blocks, it suddenly started swerving wildly. It crashed into a parked delivery truck and stopped. And all the police went running down there to arrest the thieves when they crawled dazedly out of their van.

"Wow," said Juan Green, twenty-three years old. "That was intense, wasn't it?"

"Come on," said Ruby Howard, grabbing his arm. "We need to give statements and get back to work."

"It was the strangest thing," said Detective Timothy Lawson—no relation to the warehouse clerk. "An operation planned that carefully, you'd think they'd maintain their vehicle properly, you know what I mean?"

Detective Oscar Stewart shrugged. "They always mess up," he said. "Sooner or later, on some detail, they always mess up."

"Yes, but their steering system."

"Well," said Stewart, "it was a stolen van. I suppose they just grabbed whatever was available."

"What I can't figure out," said Lawson, "is exactly what made that steering system fail like that. I mean, the mechanics say the steering fluid just vanished. Completely evaporated. Like it was superheated or something. But the engine wasn't overheating. Nothing else was wrong."

Stewart shrugged again. "We caught them. That's what matters."

"Still, it's strange. They're free and clear, heading toward the highway, and suddenly their steering fails, the fluid's gone, and there they are." Lawson shook his head. "I can't explain it."

"Don't overthink it," suggested Stewart. "They picked the wrong vehicle to steal."

"And that doesn't make sense either," said Lawson. "Why steal a van that could be identified as easily as that one?"

"Why? What was distinctive about it?"

"It was a Ford Transit, white, five years old, looked like a thousand other commercial vans. Except that on both side panels, someone had spray-painted 'Phoenix Rising' in bright orange letters you could see from a block away."

"Maybe they didn't notice when they stole it," said Stewart.

"For a well-planned operation like this one," said Lawson, "they made some really stupid mistakes. It doesn't add up."

"What do they say about it?" Stewart demanded.

"Nothing, as expected. They've lawyered up completely."

The precinct door opened, and a uniformed officer stuck his head in. "The van's owner is here," he said.

"Right," said Lawson. He followed the officer down the hall to the front desk.

The van's owner was an irritated-looking woman in her forties, tall and athletic. "Rebecca Hunt," she said. "You have my van?"

"I believe so, yes," said Lawson. "I'm afraid it's damaged."

"So I was told on the phone," said Hunt grimly. "I've already contacted my insurance."

"Good. The van's in the police impound, around back. If you'd come with me?"

On the way, Lawson said, "I understand you reported the van stolen almost immediately."

"That's right," said Hunt. "I stopped at a coffee shop on my route. I'm a medical equipment sales rep. When I came out ten minutes later, my van was gone."

"You left the keys in it?"

"Well, why not?" demanded Hunt defensively. "If I'm making just a quick stop—I never spend more than ten minutes with any customer—I always leave the keys in it. Why not?"

"The van was stolen," Lawson reminded her.

Hunt grumbled and glared. "It's always been fine until now."

"Yes, ma'am. In here."

Hunt took one look at her van and exploded. "It's destroyed! What did you do to the steering system?"

"Not a thing, ma'am. That happened during the robbery."

Hunt leaned down to examine the front wheel assembly. "Look at that! The steering fluid reservoir is bone dry, and there's residue everywhere. What did they do, drain it while driving?"

Lawson shook his head. "No, ma'am. When that happened they were three blocks from the nearest officer."

"Hmph." Hunt moved around the van, stopping short to exclaim, "What in the world is that? You didn't tell me vandals had stolen it."

"It wasn't vandals," Lawson told her. "It was four professional criminals, as I thought you knew. They were using it in a robbery."

"Then why did they do that?"

Lawson followed Hunt's pointing finger and saw again the crudely spray-painted words, "Phoenix Rising" in bright orange on both side panels. "I really don't know," he said. "It wasn't there before the van was stolen?"

"Of course not!"

Lawson frowned. "Now, why in the world would they do that?"

"I suggest," said Hunt with heavy sarcasm, "you ask them."

Lawson shook his head. "It wouldn't help. They aren't talking. I don't suppose they'll ever tell us." He looked at the side panel again. "It's the strangest thing," he said thoughtfully....

That was on Wednesday.

The Friday afternoon mail delivery to the Estoria Tribune brought an unusual letter. It was in a classic anonymous format; that is, the address had been assembled from cut-out magazine letters and glued to the envelope. There was no return address.

The letter itself was in the same format. It was brief and direct:

Dear Editor:

The Phoenix has risen. The thieves were captured. The Phoenix fights injustice. Criminals are not safe from the avenging Phoenix. WARN YOUR READERS!

Sincerely,
THE PHOENIX

The warning was duly noted, and the letter filed in the recycling bin. It didn't merit a line in the paper.

II

The warehouse robbery occurred in late September. Early in November, a man in Northfield, Dravonia went on a rampage.

It happened in a quiet suburb of Northfield, a residential area composed of modest single-family homes. The man who went on the rampage was a city planning department clerk named Ryan Wilson—a different Ryan Wilson from the one at the warehouse.

Three days before, he had been passed over for promotion for the fourth time. He called in sick and spent the three days at home, brooding, a bottle of cheap vodka constantly in his hand.

As police reconstructed it later, Wilson's wife had attempted to reason with him on the fourth morning at eight o'clock, suggesting that he really should stop wallowing and return to work. He then allegedly shoved her, and locked himself in the garage.

Mrs. Wilson then apparently called her brother, Peter Fuller, who was Ryan's brother-in-law. Fuller arrived at the house at nine-thirty, and spent considerable time knocking on the garage door, apparently requesting Wilson to unlock it and "stop acting like a child." Neighbors reported hearing Wilson shout repeatedly, "Leave me alone! Can't a man have some peace?"

At about ten-forty-five, neighbors heard gunshots from the Wilson residence, a single-story ranch house in the middle of a quiet cul-de-sac. Wilson, it was learned later, had suddenly burst from his garage, wielding a hunting rifle and, being enraged at the presence of his wife and brother-in-law, had fired several shots at them, killing his wife instantly and wounding Fuller in the arm and chest.

Fuller, wounded and terrified, staggered out the front door, crying for help and shouting, "Murder! She's dead!" At this point, neighbors called the police. One neighbor additionally contacted two local news stations, thereby earning fifty dollars in tip fees.

By coincidence, a news crew was nearby covering a city council meeting. This crew was immediately diverted to the Wilson residence, where they set up across the street and began filming with a telephoto lens.

Meanwhile, Wilson had barricaded himself in his house, firing at anything that moved.

The news crew worked frantically. One camera operator focused on the police and emergency responders and neighbors, while the other used the telephoto lens to search for Wilson. He found him occasionally, offering viewers brief glimpses of a disheveled man in jeans and a stained t-shirt, moving from window to window.

The standoff lasted nearly ninety minutes. There were police everywhere, and ambulances, and neighbors gathered at the police barricade at the end of the street, and occasionally Wilson would appear at a window and fire at someone. The police used loudspeakers to tell Wilson he should surrender, that they had the place surrounded and could wait him out. Wilson used his own voice to shout profanities back and make threats.

The police fired tear gas canisters at the house, but Wilson was able to throw most of them back out through the broken windows.

The standoff lasted nearly ninety minutes. Then it ended, suddenly and dramatically.

Wilson had appeared at a window again, apparently to fire at the news crew. All at once he screamed and dropped the rifle. The rifle clattered onto the front porch and came to rest against the railing.

Meanwhile, Wilson was running through the house, bellowing in pain. He crashed down the stairs and out the front door, stumbling, to collapse in front of the waiting police.

They had difficulty restraining him. At first they thought he was fighting them, but then one officer heard what he was screaming: "My hands! My hands are burning!"

They examined his hands. The palms and fingers were red and blistering, showing what appeared to be severe burns. There was another burn on his left cheek and another on his left shoulder.

Wilson, thoroughly subdued and confused, was taken away for medical treatment and booking. The news crew packed up and left. The neighbors returned home and posted about it on social media.

Officers had been called in from several precincts across Northfield. Among them was Detective-Sergeant Timothy Lawson, who had transferred from Valleyview just two weeks earlier. Lawson frowned thoughtfully at Wilson as he was led away, then walked over to examine the rifle.

He touched the stock, and it was slightly warm but nothing unusual.

He picked it up and turned it around. There, on the other side of the stock, burned into the wood, were crudely formed letters: "Phoenix Rising."

You don't become Police Captain without both political savvy and genuine ability. As Captain Zara Riley liked to say, you needed to be both creative—"You have to think like the criminals"—and pragmatic—"But you have to work within the system." If these were sometimes contradictory qualities, it was best not to mention it to Captain Riley.

The pragmatic side of the captain's nature was currently dominant. "What exactly are you suggesting, Lawson?" she demanded.

"I'm not entirely sure," admitted Lawson. "But we have these two incidents. First, there's the getaway van from that warehouse robbery in Valleyview. The steering fluid vanishes for no apparent reason, and someone spray-paints 'Phoenix Rising' on the sides. Then, yesterday, this man Wilson here in Northfield. He claims the rifle suddenly became too hot to hold, and he has the burn marks to prove it. And there on the rifle stock it is again: 'Phoenix Rising.'"

"He claims he carved that himself," said the captain.

Lawson shook his head. "His attorney claims he carved it. Wilson says he doesn't remember doing it. That's part of the attorney's strategy. He's building an insanity defense."

"He carved it himself, Lawson," said the captain with patient weariness. "What are you trying to prove?"

"I don't know. All I know is it's the most bizarre thing I've encountered. And what about the getaway van? What about that steering fluid disappearing?"

"It was a maintenance issue," said Riley promptly.

"The entire reservoir emptied while they were driving? And what about the graffiti on the sides?"

"How should I know?" demanded the captain. "Kids vandalized it before it was stolen, maybe. Or maybe the thieves did it themselves, who knows? What do they say?"

"They say they didn't do it," said Lawson. "And they claim they never saw it before the robbery and would have noticed if it had been there."

The captain shook her head. "I don't understand," she admitted. "What are you trying to prove?"

"I suppose," said Lawson slowly, working through it as he spoke, "I suppose I'm trying to prove that someone caused that steering failure, and made that rifle overheat, and left their signature behind."

"What? You mean like a vigilante? Come on, Lawson! What are you trying to tell me?"

"All I know," insisted Lawson, "is what the evidence shows."

"And all I know," the captain told him, "is Wilson put that mark on his rifle himself. He admits it."

"And what made it so hot?"

"Good grief, man, he'd been firing that weapon for ninety minutes! What do you think made it hot?"

"All at once?"

"He noticed it all at once, when it started burning him."

"Then how do you explain the same signature appearing both times?" Lawson asked desperately.

"How should I know? And why not? You know as well as I do these things happen. A group of activists spray-paint 'Justice Now' on a dozen buildings. It happens constantly. Why not 'Phoenix Rising'? Couldn't it occur to two people?"

"But there's no logical explanation—" started Lawson.

"What do you mean, there's no logical explanation? I just gave you the explanation. Look, Lawson, I'm busy. You have an outlandish theory—like Martinez a few years ago, remember him? Got the idea there was a serial arsonist targeting abandoned buildings. He went around trying to prove it, getting obsessed, and eventually they had to put him on administrative leave. Remember?"

"I remember," said Lawson.

"Forget this nonsense, Lawson," the captain advised him.

"Yes, ma'am," said Lawson....

The day after Ryan Wilson's rampage, the afternoon mail brought another letter to the Estoria Tribune:

Dear Editor,

You did not warn your readers. The man who shot those people could not escape the Phoenix. The Phoenix fights injustice. No criminal is safe from the Phoenix. WARN YOUR READERS.

Sincerely,
THE PHOENIX

Unfortunately, this letter was not seen by the same person who had handled the first one, two months earlier. At any rate, it was filed in the same place and forgotten.

III

New Year's Eve is an ideal time for a gang confrontation. There are too many people celebrating for the police to monitor everyone, and if you're caught carrying a weapon, well, you're just on your way to a party and you needed protection in this neighborhood.

The issue was this community center. It occupied an entire block, with entrances on two streets. The street to the east was Stonegate Crew territory, and the street to the west was Ashford Vipers territory, and both gangs claimed the community center as their turf. There had been a few minor clashes, a few members from both sides had been jumped and roughed up, but nothing major. Finally, the leaders from the two gangs had met and determined that the dispute could only be settled through confrontation.

The time was chosen: New Year's Eve. The place was chosen: the community center parking lot. The weapons were chosen: knives and chains acceptable, but no firearms. The time was set: eleven P.M. And the winner would have exclusive territorial rights to the community center, both entrances.

The night of the confrontation, the gangs assembled in their separate hangouts for final instructions. Lookouts were posted at the intersections nearest the community center, both to watch for police and to keep out any civilians who might wander through.

Ruby Howard was a lookout for the Ashford Vipers. She was seventeen years old, average height with dyed red hair and a tough demeanor. She was proud of being in the Vipers and proud of the job assigned to her. She was to watch the southwest corner.

Ruby took up her position at ten-fifty. The streets were dark and relatively quiet, most people already at parties or safely indoors. Few people ventured into this neighborhood after dark, especially on New Year's Eve. Ruby leaned against a streetlight, hands in the pockets of her Vipers jacket, and waited.

At eleven o'clock, she heard muffled sounds begin behind her. The confrontation had started.

At eleven-oh-five, a group of younger kids came walking down the street. They were all about twelve or thirteen years old, and several carried backpacks. Some wore festive hats or masks.

They started to turn toward the community center. Ruby said, "Hey, kids. Move along."

One of them, wearing a red party hat, turned to look at her. "Who, us?"

"Yes, you! Stay off that street. Go the other way."

"The bus stop's this way," objected the kid in the red hat.

"Don't care. You go around."

"Listen, lady," said the kid in the red hat, annoyed, "we need to get home."

"Yeah," said another kid, wearing a blue mask, "and we're already late."

"Not my problem," Ruby told them coldly. "You can't go down that street."

"Why not?" demanded another kid. This one wore the most elaborate costume of all: black pants and a gold shirt with a flowing black cape. He wore a black and gold mask and had a black beanie pulled down over his head. "Why can't we go that way?" this figure demanded.

"Because I said so," Ruby told him. "Now, you kids get out of here. Move."

"Hey!" cried the kid in the black-and-gold costume. "Hey, there's a fight down there!"

"It's gang business," said Ruby proudly. "You don't want to be involved."

"Hey!" cried the kid in the black-and-gold costume again. And he went running past Ruby and sprinting down the street.

"Hey, Juan!" shouted one of the other kids. "Juan, come back!"

Ruby wasn't sure what to do. If she abandoned her post to chase the one kid who'd gotten through, maybe all the others would follow. She didn't know what to do.

A sudden siren and distant flashing blue lights solved her dilemma. "Cops!" said one of the kids.

"Police!" screamed Ruby. She turned and ran down the block toward the community center, shouting, "Police! Police! Clear out, it's the cops!"

But then she stopped, stunned, when she saw what was happening in the parking lot.

The gang members from both sides were jumping around wildly, waving their arms, throwing their weapons away. Then they all started tearing off their gang jackets and throwing them away, yelling and cursing. They were making so much noise themselves that they never heard Ruby's warning. They didn't even hear the police sirens. And suddenly both parking lot entrances were filled with police officers, an officer had Ruby in custody, and the confrontation was over.

Ruby was so bewildered and frightened that everything became a blur. But in the middle of it all, she did see the small figure in the gold-and-black costume go running away down the street.

And she had the strangest feeling that it was all his fault.

Captain Zara Riley was still in her pragmatic mode this morning, and she was impatient as well. "All right, Lawson," she said. "Make it quick, I have meetings all morning. And I hope this isn't your vigilante theory again."

"I'm afraid it is, Captain," said Lawson. "Did you see this morning's paper?"

"So what?"

"Did you see the article about the gang confrontation over in the Stonegate Region?"

Captain Riley sighed. "Lawson," she said wearily, "are you going to try to connect every single incident where the word 'phoenix' appears? What's the issue with this one? These gangs have names, so what?"

"Neither one was called 'The Phoenix,'" Lawson told her. "One was the Stonegate Crew and the other was the Ashford Vipers."

"So they changed their names," said Riley.

"Both gangs? At the same time? To the same name?"

"Why not? Maybe that's what they were fighting about."

"It was a territorial dispute," Lawson reminded her. "They've admitted that. It says so in the paper. And it also says they all deny ever seeing that word on their jackets until after the fight."

"A bunch of juvenile delinquents," said Riley in disgust. "You believe them?"

"Captain, did you read the full article?"

"I skimmed it."

"All right. Here's what they claim happened: They say they started fighting at eleven o'clock. And they'd just begun when suddenly all the metal they were carrying—knives and chains and belt buckles and everything else—became freezing cold, too cold to touch. And then their leather jackets became freezing cold, so cold they had to pull them off and throw them away. And when the jackets were later collected, across the gang name on the back of each one had been burned the words 'Phoenix Rising.'"

"Now, let me tell you something," said Riley firmly. "They heard the police sirens, and they threw their weapons away. Then they threw their jackets away to try to pretend they hadn't been part of the gang fight. But they were caught before they could escape the parking lot. If the patrol cars had arrived a minute later, the parking lot would have contained nothing but weapons and jackets, and the kids would have been scattered throughout the neighborhood, innocent as can be, minding their own business. That's what happened. And all this talk about freezing cold and burned names on jackets is just some smart-aleck punk's way of mocking the police. Now, you focus on what's happening in this precinct and forget about gang fights in the Stonegate Region and comic book theories about the Phoenix, or you're going to end up like Martinez, with that arson obsession. Now, I don't want to hear any more about this nonsense, Lawson."

"Yes, ma'am," said Lawson.

But as he left the captain's office, Detective Timothy Lawson couldn't shake the feeling that something very strange was happening in their city. Three incidents, three impossible occurrences, three identical signatures. It defied logic, it defied risk management principles, it defied everything he'd learned about criminal behavior and justice theory in his years on the force.

Someone—or something—was out there. And whoever or whatever it was, they were fighting crime in a way that shouldn't be possible.

Lawson returned to his desk and pulled out the files on all three cases. He spread them across his workspace and stared at them, looking for connections, looking for patterns, looking for anything that might explain what was happening.

The steering fluid that vanished. The rifle that became too hot to hold. The metal objects that became too cold to touch. All impossible. All real. All marked with the same signature: Phoenix Rising.

He thought about the topics he'd studied in night school—applied ethics, consciousness studies, even some readings in cultural anthropology about societal change and how communities respond to threats. Was this some kind of social phenomenon? A group using technology to fight crime? But what technology could do these things?

Or was it something else entirely?

Lawson leaned back in his chair and rubbed his eyes. Captain Riley thought he was losing it, just like Martinez had. Maybe she was right. Maybe he was seeing patterns where none existed, connections that weren't there.

But he couldn't shake the feeling that something extraordinary was happening in their city. Something that defied explanation. Something that, if he could just understand it, might change everything he thought he knew about justice and how it could be served.

He looked at the files again. Three cases. Three impossible events. Three signatures.

The Phoenix was real. He was sure of it now.

He just had to prove it.
